profiles.meeting_scenario: The meeting is a design review of a national proposal for a phased rollout of biennial colorectal cancer screening using mailed FIT kits for adults aged 55-64 across eight health districts. The Ministry wants the programme introduced gradually so later-covered districts can serve as controls, and the review is focused on whether the staged rollout, evaluation frame, and reporting package are robust enough for approval before procurement begins. The agenda is to assess the proposed randomization of rollout order, what exactly counts as the control condition before crossover, and whether the evaluation tables on life-years gained per invitation and per time spent are suitable for public-health decision making. The expected outcome is a conditional approval of the current design with a short list of revisions to the proposal deck and implementation notes.

members.name: Dr. Lena Hart
members.role: Senior Evaluation Scientist, National Public Health Agency
members.expertise: Screening evaluation, causal inference, health economics, stepped-wedge and phased policy assessment
members.background: Lena is a physician-epidemiologist who spent a decade in academic public health before moving into government, where she now reviews whether national prevention programmes can support defensible claims about population benefit and efficient use of resources.
members.private_state: She wants the screening proposal to survive Treasury and parliamentary scrutiny without later accusations that the evaluation was softened for operational convenience. She is especially concerned that routine implementation decisions could quietly undermine the validity of the control comparison while still sounding methodologically acceptable in the meeting.
hidden_assumptions: A 'randomized rollout' means all districts that are not formally exempted at the national level are actually included in the random allocation pool.

A district that is 'not yet covered' should not receive programme-driven GP briefings, booking workflows, navigator staffing, or other infrastructure changes that could alter usual care before crossover.
Reporting outcomes 'per invitation' should use every invitation unit the programme deploys, including reminder letters and undeliverable mailings, because those are real intervention costs.
Relating benefit to 'time spent for the intervention' means total societal time over the screening episode, including administrative handling and downstream follow-up triggered by positive screens.

members.name: Marko Silva
members.expertise: Service rollout, regional health operations, patient communication workflows, programme logistics
members.background: Marko came from large hospital operations and now oversees implementation planning for preventive care programmes, coordinating laboratories, regional booking systems, primary care communication, and vendor timelines for national launches.
members.private_state: He wants approval to proceed without reopening the rollout calendar, because procurement slots and lab staffing plans are already fragile. He worries that overly rigid evaluation language will create delays or force district teams to hold back basic preparation work they see as harmless and necessary.
hidden_assumptions: A rollout can still be honestly described as 'randomized' even if clearly unready districts are fixed to the end and only the feasible districts are randomized.
A district becomes 'covered' when invitations are sent; backstage preparation such as GP briefings, call-center setup, and booking configuration does not count as programme exposure.
An 'invitation' is one unique eligible resident successfully reached through the validated mailing list, while reminder letters are just part of the same contact pathway.
The most decision-relevant interpretation of 'time spent for the intervention' is participant-facing time burden, because that is what affects acceptability and uptake.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a randomized rollout
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both describe the proposal as a 'randomized rollout across eight districts.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes all eight districts are in the random allocation frame unless there is a formally documented national exemption established before design approval.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes two districts can be preassigned to the final wave because of lab and staffing readiness, while the remaining six are randomized and the rollout still counts as randomized.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both view operational constraints as routine background facts rather than substantive design changes, so the phrase 'randomized rollout' feels sufficiently precise even though they are assuming different randomization sets.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in a control district before crossover
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to later-wave districts as 'not yet covered' or 'control districts.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes control districts should remain under usual care without programme-linked GP messaging, call-center scripts, booking pathways, or navigator preparation that could change behavior before invitations start.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes control districts simply should not receive invitations yet, while backend setup, GP briefings, and patient-routing preparation can begin beforehand because those steps are not public-facing screening activity.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The surface wording centers on invitations, and neither person expects backstage preparation to be controversial enough to define explicitly, so both hear 'not yet covered' as straightforward agreement.

misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means life-years gained divided by every invitation unit sent by the programme, including initial mailings, reminders, and undeliverable letters, because the denominator should reflect real intervention volume.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means life-years gained divided by each unique eligible person successfully reached after list cleaning, with reminders treated as part of the same invitation rather than separate units.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'per invitation' sounds like standard evaluation shorthand, and both think their denominator is the obvious one built into normal reporting practice, so neither notices the hidden arithmetic difference.

misalignment_points.topic: Boundary of 'time spent for the intervention'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the proposal should relate benefits to 'time spent for the intervention.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means total time consumed by the screening episode from a public-health perspective, including patient time, administrative handling, triage, follow-up coordination, and time used by downstream diagnostic work prompted by positive FIT results.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means participant-facing time burden, such as reading the letter, completing the kit, and attending any immediate screening-related appointment, because that is the time service design can directly reduce.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'time spent' feels self-explanatory, and both are focused on efficiency, but one is silently using a societal-cost frame while the other is using a user-journey frame.

turns.inner_thought: I need this package to stand up when Treasury asks whether the apparent control period was real and whether the rollout order was genuinely randomized across the whole programme. If we leave soft language in, operations will interpret it loosely and we'll be accused later of calling convenience sequencing an evaluation. I also want the efficiency tables to stay in a public-health frame, not drift into a narrower service optics exercise.
turns.utterance: Thanks, everyone. Before we move this toward sign-off, I just want to confirm that the phased FIT rollout, the control comparison, and the efficiency tables are all solid enough for ministerial approval. If those three pieces are tight, I think we're in good shape.

turns.inner_thought: I need Lena comfortable enough not to reopen the timetable. From my side this is still a randomized rollout across eight districts: the feasible six can be randomized, and the two districts that plainly cannot start in spring can sit in the final wave without changing the basic integrity of the approach. That is standard operational realism, not a redesign.
turns.utterance: Yes, that’s the plan as we’ve framed it: a randomized rollout across eight districts, delivered in three waves. North Coast and Valleyshire are already penciled into the last wave because the lab capacity there won’t be ready in spring, but otherwise the staged sequence is set up as discussed.

turns.inner_thought: All right, I’m hearing that the rollout remains randomized across eight districts in the sense that every district not formally exempted is in the allocation frame, and the two late areas must presumably be documented cleanly. The next risk is contamination: later-wave districts must stay as genuine controls, not quasi-exposed through programme machinery before crossover.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. The other point I want to pin down is how the not-yet-covered districts will operate before crossover, so the control period remains interpretable.

turns.inner_thought: She’s asking about whether we’ll hold invitations, which we will. We absolutely should still do the backend work everywhere early; otherwise the regional teams will launch unevenly and blame the evaluation for avoidable problems. To me, a district is not yet covered until invitations go out, so standardized GP briefings and booking setup beforehand are just readiness, not exposure.
turns.utterance: The not-yet-covered districts won’t start invitations until their wave. At the same time, we do want GP briefings, call-center scripts, and booking templates standardized systemwide ahead of launch, just so readiness isn’t patchy from one district to another.

turns.inner_thought: Good, so control districts remain under usual care until crossover; the readiness language can be tidied in the write-up so nobody interprets it as pre-exposure. I should move us onto the reporting tables. I’m pleased they kept life-years per invitation because, in my mind, that denominator should reflect every invitation unit the programme deploys, including reminders and failed mailings, otherwise the efficiency claim gets flattered.
turns.utterance: All right. On the evaluation deck, I was pleased to see life-years per invitation reported. That keeps the public-health efficiency framing visible, which will help when the questions turn to value rather than just uptake.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that means she’s aligned with the dashboard approach. We can calculate life-years per invitation straight off the cleaned invitee file once duplicates and failed mailings are removed; reminders are just part of the contact pathway, not separate invitations. That should make the reporting stable and easy for the operations team to maintain.
turns.utterance: Agreed. The dashboard team can populate life-years per invitation directly from the validated invitee file once duplicate addresses and failed mailings have been cleaned out. That should give us a fairly straightforward reporting line.

turns.inner_thought: I should check the time metric before this gets locked. For me, time spent for the intervention needs to capture the whole screening episode from a societal perspective: programme administration, triage, positive-result follow-up, all of it. If they only count what the participant sees, the denominator will miss the capacity burden that matters politically.
turns.utterance: And on the companion table, does the time-spent measure cover the whole intervention episode? I’m thinking particularly about whether time spent for the intervention picks up the parts that tend to consume capacity once positive FITs start flowing through.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, we’ve already got that mapped in the service-design sense: participant-facing burden across the journey. That’s the actionable piece for implementation, and the one ministers usually understand quickest when they ask whether the programme is acceptable to the public. No need to complicate it with every internal process minute.
turns.utterance: The service design team has already mapped time spent for the intervention from the participant journey. It mainly follows the letter-reading, kit completion, reminder response, and any immediate attendance steps, so we can show the burden in a way that’s easy to interpret.

turns.inner_thought: Close enough for today. I still want the wording tightened so that the randomized rollout across eight districts is described in a way that won’t invite challenge, and the notes on not-yet-covered districts need to preserve a clean control period. If those revisions are made, I can support conditional approval and sort the rest in the methods annex.
turns.utterance: Overall, this looks close. Once the wording on the randomized rollout across eight districts is tidied and the notes on the not-yet-covered districts are sharpened, I’d expect we can move this to conditional approval.

turns.inner_thought: Excellent. If the revisions stay at wording level, I can protect the rollout calendar and keep procurement moving. I’ll adjust the deck so it reflects what we’re already planning operationally, without inviting another round of redesign.
turns.utterance: That works for me. I’ll revise the deck on that basis and circulate the approval version this week so procurement can stay on schedule.
